proposals.relationship: Rodgers builds on Wiebe’s account of organizational change while treating bureaucratic social efficiency as one progressive language among several.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1982 historiographical essay,117–118 and127/n59, praises the link between organizational transformation and one strand of thought while explicitly noting that Wiebe had already made qualifications that later inquiries swamped. This specified resource coexists with Rodgers’s criticism of simplification; it does not make Wiebe responsible for Rodgers’s entire three-language interpretation. The Search for Order and later1973 essay remain unread here.
primary_locators: In Search of Progressivism,printed117–118,Wiebe paragraphs;127 concluding three-languages account;132,note59.

proposals.relationship: Rodgers argues that Wiebe’s organizational synthesis simplified progressive ideas and left the relation between professionalization and social visions insufficiently explained.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1982 essay,118–119, qualifies the new-middle-class carrier thesis and distinguishes job control from a shared bureaucratic political ethos. He praises Wiebe’s account of organizational change and later credits his earlier qualifications,n59; this is not a wholesale rejection. Hays’s more sweeping functionalist explanation is a separate target and is not silently assigned to Wiebe.
primary_locators: Printed118,from If Wiebe’s analysis through the professional-goals discussion;119 comparison to Hays;132,n59.

proposals.relationship: Rodgers disputes Hofstadter’s relatively prosperous framing of the Progressive Era, foregrounding acute labor crisis and conflict over corporate power.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1982 essay120 and note33 explicitly contrasts Hofstadter’s framing with recent labor history. David Montgomery,Bruno Ramirez and Richard Edwards retain the supporting works’ separate credit. Rodgers also treats Hofstadter’s generation as having brilliantly launched a historiographical question at114; disagreement does not erase that assessment. The original Age of Reform and all cited labor books remain unread.
primary_locators: Printed120,paragraph ending with labor crisis, and130,note33;114,opening historiographical orientation.

proposals.relationship: Rodgers uses Lears’s account of fin-de-siècle ennui as one possible explanation for the middle-class appetite for muckraking.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1982 essay124 explicitly identifies this thread with Lears and note47 specifies No Place of Grace(1981). It remains one tentative thread alongside political economy,utility monopolies and McCormick’s corruption-exposure account; no sole explanation or full agreement is claimed. Lears’s whole book remains unread.
primary_locators: Printed124,first paragraph on middle-class discovery of monopoly,Yet another thread;131,note47.

proposals.relationship: Rodgers draws on Higham’s account of Protestant social-gospel thinking as one resource for explaining progressive languages of social bonds.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1982 essay126 and note55 explicitly use this resource alongside Robert M.Crunden,Joseph F.Kett and Clyde Griffen,whose separate credit remains essential. Rodgers leaves the transatlantic reconstruction and channels of transmission open;this does not attribute the whole three-language synthesis to Higham. Higham’s original1974 article was not freshly read.
primary_locators: Printed126,first paragraph on social gospel,and131,note55 citing John Higham,Hanging Together:Divergent Unities in American History(1974),24–25.

proposals.relationship: As Soll reconstructs, Rodgers challenges the reach of Pocock’s early republican-language paradigm and calls for political, social and cultural contexts beyond it.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation: Soll2010,printed22 and notes4–6,reconstructs Rodgers1992,37–38,and retains Rodgers’s acknowledgment of the republican debate’s contribution to constitutional history. The claim is limited to the strong early paradigm,not all of Pocock’s changing work. Soll’s later criticisms of Skinner/Tuck are his own and are not assigned to Rodgers. Original1992 essay and Pocock’s books were not freshly read.
primary_locators: Soll2010,printed22,first full paragraph and notes4–6;21 for topic identity.

proposals.relationship: As Soll explains, Rodgers points to Kerber’s social and cultural history as a resource for enlarging the study of republicanism beyond political language.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation: Soll2010,22/n6 attributes this methodological use to Rodgers1992,38,and jointly credits Rhys Isaac and Sean Wilentz. Their distinct work is not collapsed into Kerber’s or asserted as a shared school. Neither Rodgers’s original1992 ending nor the particular Kerber/Isaac/Wilentz works were freshly read; Soll does not identify individual work titles in this passage.
primary_locators: Soll2010,printed22,first full paragraph,last sentence and note6 referring to Rodgers38.

proposals.relationship: As Richard J. Ross explains, Rodgers follows Williams’s keyword method while shifting attention toward the political uses and consequences of contested terms.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation: Ross1998,230,note1,contrasts genealogy with Rodgers’s forensic emphasis and points to Contested Truths(1987),3–16. The note cites Williams’s revised1983 Keywords; its historical edition is not silently changed. Only this substantive introductory note was read in a public reproduced/indexed extract; direct Yale retrieval returned403. Neither complete article nor Rodgers’s and Williams’s books were freshly read.
primary_locators: Richard J.Ross,Memorial Culture,printed230,note1,especially sentences beginning Following Williams’s lead and How were political concepts;public Paperity transcription.
